idiom_name: withTaskGroup + addTask/next (structured concurrency); DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform for the blocking form
implementation_notes: Swift 5.5 structured concurrency is the direct realization: withTaskGroup creates the child tasks, addTask fans them out and the group always waits for every child before returning - the join is enforced by the language - while iterating the group (or next()) yields results in completion order and is the aggregation point. async let is the fixed-arity form. Before async/await, the pattern was DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform(iterations:) over a global queue or an OperationQueue with maxConcurrentOperationCount for the worker bound; those remain the choice for purely blocking work.
pitfalls: The group waits for all children even after an early return; cancelAll() only signals, so children must check Task.isCancelled cooperatively.
A TaskGroup (and its child results) cannot escape the withTaskGroup body, and results arrive in arbitrary order.
The cooperative thread pool is sized to the cores: blocking calls (semaphores, synchronous I/O) inside tasks can exhaust it and stall unrelated work.
